Probable Fatal Shooting.
This morning a party of colored people went to Milan from Moline to fish. Among the number was Barney Cleveland, the barber, and who when drunk is a terror. The party reached Milan without trouble and all except Barney angled for fish. The latter thought he must have a good time up town, so he left the party and sauntered along Main street, Milan. He was boisterous and unruly and before long got into difficulty with James Alex, ander, of Rural. While the fraus was at its height, Special Officer Lever, interfered and ordered Cleaveland to desist. Instead of complying, Cleaveland, abused the officer and resisted arrest. The officer called on others to assist, among them Robert Keeler, and again ordered Cleaveland to surrender. Cleaveland refused, however, and began throwing rocks at the officer, one narrowly missing him, and another slightly grazing Mr. Keeler. The officer was determined to take Cleaveland, who was swearing at a terrific rate and hurling rocks at everyone who came in his way. As a last resort the officer told Cleveland if he did not halt and surrender he would shoot. The answer was a rock from the pugnacious negro, which nearly struck the officer in the head. Officer Lever then fired two shots at Cleveland both of which took effect—one in the stomach near the pit and the other in the abdomen, just below the navel, which brought Cleveland to the ground and he was taken in. All of this happened about noon within a few rods of the Milan House, and created great excitement at the time, Public sentiment is with the officer, who used every means possible to arrest Cleveland peaceably but without avail. Had the officer not shot him, the chances are that Keeler and the officer would have been hurt for Cleveland is one of the worst cases, when drunk, in the county. A few years ago Officer Teller, of Moline, undertook to arrest Barney Cleveland, but he was resisted, Teller pounded Barney's head fearfully before he took him, but he took him down. Another time Special Officer Wormly tried to arrest Cleveland and he bit Wormley's thumb to the bone. Another time Barney was hauled in by the Rock Island police, and had to be liberally clubbed before he would go to jail.

Barney Cleveland, when sober is peaceable enough, is a good barber and has a good trade, but when he gets on a tear there is not a more wickedly devilish man anywhere. He is the most powerful built fellow of his inches in the county, and has many times thrashed three men in succession.

It is believed he cannot survive, as the wounds are in his stomach. He has a large family, has lived in Moline a great many years, and has probably seen the inside of the calaboose as often as any one in the three cities.

When we last heard from Milan, Cleveland was sinking and his death is expected, He can hardly recover.

INCENDIARISM.

INCENDIARISM.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
MILWAUKEE, Aug. 7.—The fourth attempt within a year to burn the Grand Opera-House was made this morning. The fire was started in the basement of McLaughlin's liquor store. The incendiary entered through an unfastened window. A barber next door discovered the smoke and got the Department out in time to save the building. The loss on the whisky and wines is $8,000 to $10,000; that to the building is about $1,000. The stock is insured in the following Companies: Western of Toronto, Rhode Island Association, Orient of Hartford, Fairfield of Connecticut, and Metropole of Paris. Who it is that wants to burn the Opera-House, and what the object, is a mystery.

BALBO'S FUNERAL.

NEW YORK, Aug. 7.—The funeral of Pietro Balbo, the Italian executed Friday for wifemurder, took place to-day from the undertaker's. There was an immense crowd of spectators. The remains were not exposed to view. Six pall-bearers represented as many Italian Societies. There were forty carriages in line. Fathers Anacletus and Julius, and Balbo's counsel, accompanied the remains to Calvary Cemetery, where the interment took place. The societies were not allowed by the police to carry draped flags. They formed in procession, and accompanied the body to the Brooklyn ferry.

STABBING AFFRAY.

MILWAUKEE. Wis., Aug. 7.—Mathew Krause and Ernst Land, two young farmers of the Town of Two Creeks, this county, got into a quarrel at that place Thursday evening, which resulted in Land's stabbing Krause seven times in different parts of his body with his pocket-knife. Krause was probably fatally injured, and at last accounts was thought to be dying. Land was brought here and lodged in jail to await an examination.

MURDERED HER LOVER.

NEWBERNE, N. C., Aug. 7.—Great excitement was created here to-day by the arrest of Miss Elizabeth Hill on the charge of having murdered John Lawrence, her affianced, in Edgecombe County, in 1878. The young man died very suddenly, and there are witnesses now who swear that the woman grew tired of him, and to rid herself of his company poisoned him.

SHOT BY AN OFFICER.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
DAVENPORT, Ia., Aug. 7.—This evening a colored man named Barney Cleaveland was shot by a police officer at Milan. The officer was attempting to arrest him when he picked up a rock, and the policeman shot him twice in the lower part of the abdomen. Cleaveland lies in a very critical condition.

THE SHOOTING OF BARNEY
CLEVELAND.
A Despicable Attempt to make Political Capital out of the affair,
A Despicable Attempt to make Political Capital out of the affair,

The Argus in the article citing the shooting of Barney Cleveland, on Saturday, by Officer Leber, at Milan, stated that the wounded man would die, and at 1 o'clock this morning, he breathed his last. He had every possible attention, but the wounds were beyond human skill to heal, and at the hour named Barney Cleveland was dead.

Coroner Morris was notified and at 8.30 o'clock began the inquest. An effort was made to create a partisan line by some small minded Republicans in Milan, and as evidence of it, some self-styled friends of the deceased, objected to any Democrats being placed on the jury and several were objected to on that account. The jury was finally made up, composed of five Republicans and one Democrat—George M. Dickson, and the examination of witnesses began.

It was evident that some of the bigoted partisans were going to make political capital out of the affair if possible, and in giving testimony, one witness, whose name we did not learn, proceeded to give his opinions as well as evidence and also threw in a few words of advice. His bias was so flagrant that Coroner Morris promptly squelched him, saying, "We don't want your opinions, sir, nor your prejudices, but we want the facts." He was proceeding to work on the partisan line, and was summarily shut up by Coroner Morris, who again reminded him that the case was being tried by a jury of intelligent men, and the verdict would be given in accordance with facts—not prejudice or opinions.

At 10 A. M. five witnesses had been examined, and at 3 P. M. the inquest was still proceeding. Thus far the preponderance of evidence is on the side of the officer, who seems to have done no more than his duty.

The attempt of certain small minded Republicans to create a partisan feeling because Cleveland, the dead man, was colored, is despicable and reprehensible. It is going rather far when the partisan line is carried to a coroner's inquest, and THE ARGUS is glad to note that Coroner Morris so peremptorily shut down on the attempt to create'a prejudice against the officer by drawing the party line, Coroner Morris had the good sense to see that an attempt of this sort would be damaging, if the bigoted partisans of Milan did not.

THE ARGUS is not in possession of all the facts but the incidents stated are vouched for by those who speak from positive knowledge.

It is futile to endeavor to make party capital out of this affair—as well condemn any officer, who, in the discharge of his duty is compelled to use a pistol. THE ARGUS does not know what Officer Lever is politically, nor does it care, it simply knows from the facts thus far adduced that he did his duty and for that he is entitled to a fair hearing.

The Shooting of Barney Cleveland
In the coroners inquest on the death of Barney Cleveland, particulars of which were given in THE ARGUS of yesterday, the jury arrived at a verdict late in the day that "Bernard Cleveland came to his death by revolver shot wounds from the hand of Policeman S. The verdict justifying the action of Officer Leever, in the discharge of his duty, was received with much satisfaction by the community.

A mob of horsemen took John Bailz, who murdered his wife in May, 1879, from the jail at Athens, Ka., on the night of the 7th inst., and hung him. Bailz had been twice sentenced to death, and each time granted a new trial.

Thomas E. Snellbaker, fatally shot Policeman A. Chumley, while under arrest, at Cincinnati, O., on the 8th inst., for disorderly conduct.

Barney Cleveland, a colored man, was shot dead by an officer at Milan, Ia., on the 7th, while resisting arrest.

R. L. Edwards, a preacher, was called out of his residence at Galveston, Texas, on the night of the 5th inst., and shot dead by unknown parties.

At Oldtown, Craighead county, Ark., a few days since, John F. Klingensmith, agent of Streight & Co., of Indianapolis, Ind., was killed by Calvyn Smith—by blows from behind with a gun. Both men were engaged in getting out timber, and had a quarrel of two years standing, which originated in business rivalry.

On the evening of the 5th inst., Woodson L. Gunnels, a well-to-do farmer living 20 miles west of Americus, Ga., left home to visit a sick neighbor and returning home at ten o'clock at night, found his wife and nine of his ten small children in a horrible sleep from the effects of morphine administered in lemonade by Mrs. Gunnels. A note in a handwriting of Mrs. Gunnel was found under the morphine on the table, in which she stated that she had deliberately administered morphine to the children and herself with the intention of destroying them all and that she was not actuated by any domestic trouble. Medical aid was immediately summoned, but Mr. Gunnels soon died, and no hopes of recovery are entertained for three of the children. The others are believed to be out of danger.

At May Lick, Ky., on the 3d inst., Perry Jefferson was fatally shot by two negroes who were subsequently lynched.

An American missionary and his American servant, while on the road to relieve the famished population, were found with their throats out, near Ismidd, Turkey, recently. The murderers were arrested. They are two nomad Turks, and confessed the crime.

A row occurred in John Sullivan's saloon at Chicago, on the 3d inst., between the proprietor and a French sailor named Bourgoum. In the melce the latter was struck in the chest by a beer keg in the hands of Sullivan's wife. All the parties were arrested. Next morning Bourgoum was found dead in his cell. Mrs. Sullivan is held for murder.

Dennis Hayes, a milkman, was shot dead at San Francisco, Cal., on the 4th inst., by Michael Dolan, in a trifling altercation.

At San Francisco, Cal., on the 4th inst., James Cahill, an assayer, fired a harmless shot at Mrs. N. Sheline and then shot himself through the head.

Epististe Ferschneider, cook at the United States hotel, Saratoga, was shot dead on the night of the 3d inst., by his friend and roommate August Bremner. Another case of playfully pointing a pistol.

At Sherman, Texas, in an altercation on the 4th inst., a man named Weaver stabbed and killed a neighbor named Cox. Both farmers.

Deputy Sheriff Will F. Garrett was shot and instantly killed in a house of ill-repute at Galveston, Texas, by W. P. Allen, whom Garrett was about to arrest.

W. W. Taylor, deputy sheriff, attempted the arrest of Martin L. Minnott, a notorious desperado, at Montague, Texas, on the 3d inst. Minnott tried to shoot Taylor, but missed his aim and was killed instantly by the officer.

A negro at Savannah, Ga., saw a young colored girl with whom he had quarreled, in the custody of an officer on the 3d inst., and going up to her, placed a revolver to her temple and fired, killing her instantly.

Clinton Montague, an employ of Lasher's brewery, was found dead on the night of the 2d inst., at Crawfish Bottom, Frankfort, Ky., with a bullet through his head. No clue to the murder.

Early on the morning of the 3d inst., a burglar entered the premises of John McMahon, a saloon keeper, at Chicago. The latter was awakened by the noise and called out from the bedroom, when the fiend advanced to the bedside, placed the muzzle of the revolver to McMahon's right breast and fired. The bullet entered his body just above the nipple, and McMahon fell back dead. The murderer escaped.

CRIMES AND CASUALTIES—BY TELEGRAPH.
BOY KILLED BY AN ELEVATOR.
SALT LAKE, Utah, Aug. 18.—A twelve-years-old son of N. C. Flygare was crushed to death to-day by the falling of an elevator page.

KILLED BY A FALL.
DENVER, Col., Aug. 18.—At Pueblo, Col., yesterday, Henry Orr, a railroad employee engaged in driving piles, fell against the point of a crowbar and was killed instantly.

KILLED BY A LOCOMOTIVE.
ELIZABETHPORT, N. J., Aug. 18.—L. Fox, an old resident of Elizabeth, was killed this morning, by being struck by the engine of the Long Branch train at Elizabeth port.

THE FUSE TOO SHORT.
WILKESBARRE, Penn., Aug. 18.—John Manson, a miner, was instantly killed to-day, while dring a blast in a mine at Sugar Notch. He made the fuse too short and could not escape.

AN ALABAMA MURDER.
MOBILE, Ala., Aug. 18.—Last night at Whistler, five miles from here, a negro named James Kelly was shot and instantly killed by a creole man Antone Hennenberg at a colored fair.

TWO BROTHERS DROWNED.
PITTSTON, Penn., Aug. 18.—Beanie and Joe Frick, brothers, eight and eleven years old respectively, while playing in a boat on the Sauguchanna River, this morning, fell overboard and were drowned.

DROWNED WHILE CATCHING CRABS.
BAYVILLE, N. J., Aug. 18.—Benjamin Tumson was drowned this morning at Sandy Creek, it is supposed while out crabbing. He was visiting here from Springfield, Otsego County, N. Y., and was about thirty years of age.

A BODY FISHED UP.
CARTHAGE, N. Y., Aug. 18.—A boy fishing in the river this morning, hauled up the body of a man about thirty years old, supposed to be that of Patrick Miloy. The body had been in the water probably ten days. Miloy was of temperate habits.

ATTEMPT TO POISON A FAMILY.
PHILADELPHIA, Penn., Aug. 18.—Agnes C. Riddle, age 14, a servant in the employ of John C. Macy, is charged with attempting to poison Mrs. Macy and two male coarders, by placing oxic acid in their coffee. Physicians counteracted the effect, but Mrs. Macy suffered intensely.

KILLED IN SELF DEFENCE.
CHICAGO, Ill., Aug. 18.—Freeman F. Gross shot and killed Michael Fleming, at No. 103 Ewing st., last night. Gross was attracted by cries of distress, and found Fleming striking Mrs. Fleming with a chair. On Gross's appearance Fleming turned on him, and Gross, being hard pressed, fired two shots.

BOLD RIVER PIRATES.
ST. LOUIS, M. J., Aug. 18.—The Post-Dispatch has private advises from Ashport, where the steamer Vicksburg recently sank. River pirates were discovered last night carrying off the cargo. The crew fired at the thieves, and one of them is supposed to have been killed. Later a band of masked men captured the wrecking boat, placed Mr. Bedard under guard on the boat, and took the rest of the crew to the shore. Great excitement exists.

Such phenomenal ratios of increase as these of Nebraska, Kansas, Colorado and Oregon are due to the fact that the population of these States in 1870 was so small that the gain of a few hundred thousand immigrants constitutes an enormous ratio of increase. According to this, the rate of increase of the South has exceeded that of the rest of the Union, and its gain of population is between five hundred and six hundred thousand greater than that of the Western States. Virginia, Missouri and Kentucky, gain more than Indiana, Wisconsin, Iowa or Nebraska. The increase in Virginia, Kentucky and North Carolina exceeds anything ever known in the census reports, as will be seen from the following comparison:

Kentucky, 1840 to 1850, 202.57; 1850 to 1860, 162.856; 1860 to 1870, 166.326; 1870 to 1880, 413.320; Virginia, 1840 to 1850, 94.088; 1850 to 1860, 100.282; 1860 to 1870, 5.533; 1870 to 1880, 374.837; North Carolina, 1840 to 1850, 115.620; 1850 to 1860, 123.583; 1860 to 1870, 78.739; 1870 to 1880, 318.152.

The gain of population in Virginia, for seventy years prior to 1880, was only 423.555. According to the census, her gain in the last decade was 374.837. The two Virginias comprised one state prior to 1863. Taking the populations of the two together, we find that they have increased from 1,667,177 in 1870 to 2,308,000 in 1880. Who would have supposed that population was pouring into North Carolina faster than into Wisconsin and Nebraska, and nearly as fast as into Indiana and Minnesota? And who would have thought that Kentucky would show a greater gain in population than any state in the North, the West or on the Pacific slope, with the exception of Illinois? The census returns certainly show up well for the "solid South." If the present basis of representation should be preserved, the sixteen Southern states would gain twenty eight congressmen, while the remaining twenty two states would gain forty seven. If the census returns are to be believed, the South is the most progressive section of the country; but the reports of the marvelous increase of population in a number of Southern states are received with such incredulity that there is a general cry in the Northern and Western States for a re-enumeration."

[Certainly! We "rebels" must be kept down in some way or other. If in no other way, then let these census enumerators be removed, and others appointed to make a "stalwart" enumeration, and one that will suit such people as are in the "Northern and Western States," that the American talks of. When we consider that these enumerators were nominated to the Senate by Mr. Hayes, upon the recommendation of General Walker, the Superintendent of the Census, and that at least four fifths of them are republicans, it seems that these people of the "Northern and Western States" have lost confidence in the well known characteristics of their partizans. As for us, we welcome a re-enumeration; for if the census was taken as carelessly throughout the South as it was in some parts of this city, we of the South will be largely the gainers in population by it.

"CUTAGES."—On Saturday last the negroes of Kert county, Del, had their annual frolic on Bower's Beach. Mirth and jollity prevailed during the day, but the return in the evening was marked by a murder. On the road two wagons stopped to water horses, and a quarrel and fight ensued between the occupants, who were mostly inflamed with bad whiskey. One crowd, headed by Burt Johnson, of Camden, assaulted the other wagon, and Nicholas Mosely, one of the negroes, was shot in the head, causing his death before morning.

At a colored fair near Mobile, Ala., Tuesday night, James Kelly, colored, was shot and killed by Anton Henneberg, a creole. A young colored man named Alexander was arrested at Mobile yesterday for cutraging two colored women.
